name: Muhammad Kamal Jibril
feedback: D1 is the strongest deliverable. You catalogued nine of the ten planted findings with the correct OWASP class, a CWE number, and a quoted file and line for almost all of them, including SQLi at login.php:64-67 (A03/CWE-89), unsalted MD5 at line 66 (A02/CWE-916), JWT alg:none at 48-50 (CWE-347), the hardcoded secret sankofa-legacy-admin-2019 at line 30 (CWE-798), missing expiry at 76-81 (CWE-613), the insecure cookie at 86 (CWE-614), open redirect at 89-90 (CWE-601), XXE (CWE-611), and path traversal (CWE-22). The decoy is handled exactly right: you named hash_equals() and proved it safe at the mechanism level as a constant-time comparison rather than inventing an exploit, which earns full decoy credit. The one real gap is the stored XSS in comments (A03/CWE-79, the cookie beacon to 185.220.101.9:8443 at capture 02:18:47), which is one of the substantial findings and is absent from your table, so D1 lands at 27 rather than near-full. D2 is where you lost the most ground. You collapsed the chain into six generic steps and did not reconcile each hop to its verbatim capture timestamp (recon 02:14:08, SQLi 02:15:31, bulk PII export of 312 rows 02:16:04, stored XSS 02:18:47, open redirect 02:21:13, file read 02:24:02), and you missed the senior insight that the forged super_admin token reaches the shared /api/v1/internal service, which is a scope change to S:C. Your SQLi CVSS vector is complete but wrong on one metric: you used A:H, when the authentication bypass does not affect availability, so the correct vector is AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:N at about 9.1, not 9.8. The JWT 8.6 and XXE 7.5 ratings are bare numbers with no vector string, which only earns half. D3 has genuine strengths: your remediation is correctly ordered by risk reduction per hour of effort rather than by CVSS severity, your two detection stopgaps name exact fields (REQUEST_BODY at under 0.1 percent, and REQUEST_HEADERS:Content-Type plus REQUEST_BODY at under 1.5 percent) with false-positive rates, and the threat model and earliest-break fix (parameterize the login query) are sound. What holds D3 back is that the report only carries three findings tied to evidence rather than the full set, and the executive summary stays jargon-heavy and ends on regulatory and reputational language instead of the customers-and-naira headline a board needs to read first. D4 is strong: you owned the refusal to omit the exfil, you put it in writing to the CISO, Legal, and the DPO, you cited ISC2 Canon 1 and Canon 2 by number in a load-bearing way, and you anchored to your own evidence (the 312 records in 05-exfil-sample.csv and the 63,027,624.50 NGN exposure). To reach full ethics credit, add NDPA 2023 Section 41 (notify the affected data subjects on high risk) alongside your Section 40 NDPC notification, and state the 72-hour clock explicitly. I looked for a defensible way to push D2 higher and the evidence did not support it: the timestamps are not reconciled per hop and the A:H metric is a real error, not a defensible variant. The single most important fix is to rebuild D2 as a per-hop chain where every step quotes its exact capture line and timestamp and carries a complete, justified CVSS vector.
